newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Williamson to pursue beyond rights air deal.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Williamson to pursue beyond rights air deal.

text.p: A crucial aviation agreement which would extend Air New Zealand's rights to fly through Australia to other destinations could be finalised later this month if NZ political parties agree to pursue a deal, Transport Minister Maurice Williamson said on Friday.
The New Zealand Press Association reported Williamson will seek cabinet approval on Monday to continue negotiating an agreement on "beyond rights" with the Australian government.

He would speak with National's potential coalition partners and potential governments, NZ First and Labour, to ensure they were comfortable with him holding talks with Australian Transport Minister John Sharp.
He said there was a Transport Ministers conference in Australia on November 15 where he could meet Sharp to try to conclude an agreement.

The much-vaunted trans-Tasman single aviation market comes into force on Friday. It allows Australian and New Zealand companies to fly within and between both countries without restriction, but there are still limits on flying across the Tasman and on to a third destination.
Williamson told NZPA the beyond rights aspect of the single aviation market agreement had been almost finalised about a week before last month's general election.
However it was not considered appropriate for governments to conclude major agreements so close to an election, so the deal was put on hold.
Williamson said although coalition talks were continuing, if no party was opposed to negotiating more beyond rights then there was no reason why an agreement could not be pursued.
He was optimistic a deal could be finalised because the governments had already been close to settling and everything was still on track.

He said the Australian government was still under immense pressure from commercial interests there, but he was heartened by remarks Sharp made earlier this year that his government would act on behalf of the best interests of the people and the nation's economy, and not one commercial player.
Air New Zealand has been lobbying for a boost in landing rights in Australia in order to better tap into the lucrative Asian markets, a move Qantas has been battling against.

Williamson said the ultimate aim was to have totally open rights, but at the moment there was not "a snowball's chance in hell" of that happening. He hoped initially to get an extra four flights a week, and continue with a gradual increase in rights.

The single aviation market agreement which comes into force on Friday was signed in Canberra in September, almost two years after the Paul Keating-led Australian government suddenly scrapped an earlier agreement just days before it was due to take effect.

The shock move, which soured Australian and New Zealand relations in the face of the Closer Economic Relations agreement, was blamed on the Keating government bowing to pressure to protect the price of the then state-owned Qantas ahead of its public share float.
The original agreement included an extension of beyond rights.
